title: Hotel Interieur Ontwerp Trends: How Hotel Interior Design Is Evolving
description: Explore hotel interieur ontwerp trends: living-room lobbies, local character, biophilic design and smart tech shaping modern hotel interiors.
body_html:
"Hotel interieur ontwerp" — Dutch for hotel interior design — is going through one of its most interesting periods in decades. The old formula of a formal reception desk, a corridor of identical rooms and a breakfast hall tucked away behind frosted glass no longer matches how guests actually behave. Travelers today judge a hotel less by its star rating and more by how it feels: whether the lobby invites them to linger, whether the design tells them something about the city outside, and whether the technology works quietly in the background instead of getting in the way.

The trends shaping hotel interiors right now cluster around four big ideas: the lobby reimagined as a living room, a deep commitment to local character, biophilic design that brings nature indoors, and technology integrated so smoothly that it almost disappears. Below we walk through each of these directions, plus the material and layout choices that support them, so you can recognize what good contemporary hotel design looks like — whether you are commissioning a project, renovating a property, or simply gathering ideas for your own interior.

The Lobby as a Living Room

The most visible shift in hotel interieur ontwerp is happening at the front door. Lobbies used to be transactional spaces: check in, collect a key, move on. Now they are designed as social living rooms where guests work on laptops in the morning, meet colleagues in the afternoon and drink cocktails at night. The reception desk shrinks — sometimes to a simple standing pod — and the reclaimed floor area fills with clusters of lounge seating, communal tables, library shelves and a bar or coffee counter that stays active all day.

Designing a lobby this way changes the economics of the ground floor. Instead of dead space that guests hurry through, the lobby becomes a revenue-generating venue that also attracts locals, which in turn makes the hotel feel alive. The design cues come from residential interiors: layered rugs, table lamps instead of only overhead lighting, bookshelves, art you would plausibly find in a home. The goal is for a guest to sit down without feeling like they are loitering in a corporate hall.

Local Character and a Sense of Place

International consistency was once the selling point of large hotel brands; today it is often a liability. Guests increasingly want the interior to answer a simple question: where am I? Hotels respond by weaving local identity into the design — commissioning regional artists, using materials with local provenance, referencing the building's history, and echoing the architectural language of the surrounding streets.

In the Netherlands, for example, a hotel might draw on the tall windows, brick facades and pragmatic elegance of Dutch canal houses — a tradition explored in our overview of Dutch architecture. Elsewhere in Europe, designers borrow from local classicism, art nouveau or industrial heritage; our guide to European architecture styles is a useful primer on those vocabularies. The strongest projects avoid clichés: instead of hanging a windmill photo, they might use a color palette drawn from the local landscape or restore original structural elements and leave them visible.

Biophilic Design: Nature Indoors

Biophilic design — the practice of connecting interiors to nature — has moved from a niche idea to a baseline expectation in hospitality. Guests spend most of their stay indoors, often after long travel, and interiors rich in plants, daylight and natural materials measurably soften that experience.

In hotels, biophilia shows up at several scales:

  • Planting: living green walls in lobbies, large sculptural trees in atriums, and hardy potted species in guest rooms and corridors.
  • Daylight: layouts that pull natural light deep into the plan, skylights over courtyards, and window seats that make daylight a destination.
  • Materials: timber, stone, rattan, linen and clay finishes that age gracefully and feel warm to the touch.
  • Views and airflow: orienting seating toward gardens or water, and using operable windows or terraces where climate allows.

The trend pairs naturally with sustainability goals: natural ventilation, durable materials and daylighting reduce energy use while improving how the space feels.

Quiet Technology Integration

Technology in hotels has matured past the gadget phase. The current direction is invisible convenience: mobile check-in that lets the lobby be a lounge rather than a queue, keyless room entry, lighting and climate scenes controlled from a bedside panel or the guest's own phone, and abundant, well-placed charging. Meeting spaces get wireless presentation tools; rooms get streaming-friendly televisions that pair with personal devices instead of locking guests into a proprietary menu.

Good design hides the hardware. Cables disappear into joinery, speakers sit behind fabric panels, and controls are simplified to a few intuitive choices. The test of well-integrated hotel technology is that guests only notice it when they need it — and that a less technical guest can still turn off the lights without reading a manual.

Guest Rooms: Calm, Compact, Considered

Guest room design is trending toward calm minimalism with a few generous gestures. Rather than filling rooms with furniture, designers invest in one exceptional bed, one good chair, excellent blackout and acoustic performance, and a bathroom that feels more spa than utility. Compact rooms — a necessity in expensive city centers — borrow tricks from small-apartment design: wall-mounted nightstands, wardrobes replaced by open rails and hooks, and desks that double as vanities.

Color palettes lean warm and muted, with texture doing the work that pattern used to do: boucle headboards, lime-washed walls, wood veneer, brushed metal. The intent is a room that photographs beautifully but, more importantly, lowers the guest's pulse when the door closes.

Traditional Versus Contemporary Hotel Interiors

ElementTraditional approachContemporary direction
LobbyFormal reception desk, pass-through spaceLiving-room lounge, café/bar, co-working
IdentityUniform brand standard everywhereLocal materials, art and architectural references
NatureDecorative flower arrangementsGreen walls, daylighting, natural material palettes
TechnologyVisible gadgets, proprietary systemsMobile keys, ambient controls, hidden hardware
Guest roomsFull furniture sets, heavy draperyFewer, better pieces; texture-led calm palettes

Trying These Ideas Yourself

You do not need a hospitality budget to borrow from hotel interieur ontwerp. The living-room lobby translates directly into open-plan homes: layered seating, a coffee station, lamps at multiple heights. Biophilic moves — plants, natural textiles, daylight-first layouts — work in any room.
